messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Writer
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun is a 20-year-old South Asian American man who came to treatment several months after the sudden death of a loved one, at a point when his life had become organized around bracing for more loss and trying not to be reminded of the one that had already happened. He is single and works as a writer, a job he once imagined as a place of freedom and absorption. Before the death, he described himself as light, funny, and future-oriented, someone who could lose an afternoon drafting scenes, making plans for what he wanted to publish, and talking easily with friends about what came next. Now, when he looks back on that version of himself, he feels as if he is describing someone else. He had come to believe that he used to be a happy person but now was simply miserable, and what disturbed him almost as much as the grief was the sense that the basic rules he once trusted no longer applied.

The death was abrupt enough that it split time for him into before and after. One day the person was alive and still part of the ordinary structure of his days; then, without warning, they were gone. In the first days afterward, Arjun found himself waiting for the world to correct itself, as if there had been some mistake. Instead, each practical reminder forced the finality back on him. He learned quickly how much of everyday life could turn into a reminder of the person he had lost. Objects in the home, old messages, familiar foods, a phrase someone else used in the same tone, even the shape of an ordinary evening could confront him with the absence. Those moments did not feel bittersweet to him; they felt unbearable, like being pushed up against the fact of the death all over again. He began moving away from anything that might evoke that person. If friends brought them up gently, he redirected the conversation. If he came across belongings, photos, or places linked to the loss, he left the room or found some reason to busy himself elsewhere.

As the weeks went on, the death altered more than what he could bear to look at. It changed the way he understood safety itself. He was certain now that the world was dangerous in a way he had previously been naive about. Other people still seemed able to talk about next semester, future jobs, trips, relationships, and deadlines as though life would continue in an orderly sequence. Arjun could not do it. Making plans for the future came to feel almost irrational, even tempting fate. When someone asked what he wanted to do later in the year or where he saw his writing going, he would go quiet or answer vaguely. It was not indecision in the ordinary sense. He felt that whatever stability people imagined they had could be taken away without warning, and he no longer believed in a world where effort or goodness offered any protection. He described his beliefs about how the world works as having been completely destroyed.

This sense of threat followed him into ordinary moments. Even in places he knew were safe, he could not relax. Sitting at his desk to write, he stayed physically tense, shoulders raised, attention repeatedly pulled away from the page by noises in the apartment hallway or outside on the street. Small sounds that would once have faded into the background now made him jump—a door shutting in another room, a phone dropping onto a table, the sudden buzz of an appliance. Nights were especially difficult. He had trouble falling asleep and, when he did sleep, he woke easily, alert and restless, as if his body had decided that letting go was no longer wise. The exhaustion made writing harder, and the difficulty concentrating turned his work into something strained and stop-start. Deadlines slipped. He told himself he would return to projects once he felt more like himself, but he no longer trusted that version of himself to come back.

In his relationships, Arjun had started asking others again and again to tell him that he was okay. He texted friends after bad nights, called family members to hear them say he sounded fine, and looked for some certainty in their voices that he could not generate on his own. The reassurance helped briefly, but only briefly. What frightened him most was not just that someone he loved had died, but that this had revealed something terrible and permanent about life—that no one was really safe, that happiness was flimsy, and that he himself had been changed beyond repair.

By the time he sought help, his world had narrowed markedly. He was avoiding reminders of the person he lost, shrinking from conversations about the future, sleeping poorly, startling at ordinary sounds, and living in a constant state of strain. The immediate reason he came in was that he could see the cost in the life he was supposed to be building: he was writing less, answering people less, and feeling less recognizable to himself each week. He said he wanted help because he could not keep living as if every day were waiting to be shattered again. At the same time, he was afraid that talking directly about the death would make it feel even more real, and afraid that if he ever let himself relax, something else terrible would happen.
